captions: This is a real stock portfolio — worth fifty-nine
thousand rupees.
Seven holdings. Some winning, some losing.
But how do you actually judge a stock?
In the next few minutes, we'll learn to read
one like a professional — from the very beginning.
Every stock can be judged two ways.
The first lens is fundamental analysis. It asks a
simple question — is the business good, and is
the price fair?
It looks at how much a company earns, how
well it earns it, and what you pay for
that.

The second lens is technical analysis. It ignores
the
business, and asks — what is the price actually
doing?
The trend, the momentum, the timing.

Great investors use both. Let's start with the
first.
Part one. Fundamentals.
The health of the business behind the share —

earnings, quality, and value. Let's build it from
zero.
First, what is a share?
It's one tiny slice of a real company. Buy
one share of HDFC Bank, and you own a
sliver of that bank — its profits, and its
risks.

Today, one slice costs seven hundred and twenty
rupees.
Multiply that price by the total number of shares,
and you get the market cap — how big
the whole company is.

That size sorts the market into small-caps,
mid-caps, and
large-caps. HDFC Bank is a large-cap.
Now the most famous number in investing — the
P, E.
First, earnings per share, or E P S. That's

the company's yearly profit, split across every
share.
The P E is just the price divided by
that profit.
It tells you how many rupees you pay for
one rupee of yearly profit.

HDFC Bank at seven-twenty, with about fifty-one
rupees of
profit per share, trades near fourteen times.
In plain terms — you pay fourteen rupees for
one rupee of profit. Roughly fourteen years to earn
it back. Lower is usually cheaper.
Next, price to book.
Book value is what a company would be worth
if you sold everything and paid off every debt
— its net worth, per share.
Price to book is the price divided by that
net worth.
Below one means you're buying it for less than
its own assets.
It matters most for banks. HDFC Bank trades near
one point eight times its book — a fair
price for a quality lender.

Here's the one that separates great businesses from
average
ones — return on equity.

It's the yearly profit divided by the shareholders'
money
in the business.
It answers — for every hundred rupees the owners
put in, how much profit comes back each year?

Infosys earns about thirty-two rupees on every
hundred. That's
a thirty-two percent return on equity.

High, consistent returns are a compounding engine —
the

single biggest sign of a quality business. Its
cousin,
return on capital, tells the same story.
Three quick health checks.
Debt to equity — how much the company borrows
against its own money. Low is safer.
Promoter holding — how much the founders still own.
High means their skin is in the game with
yours.
And dividend yield — the cash the company pays
you each year, as a percent of the price.
Together, these tell you if the balance sheet is
sound and the owners are aligned.
A cheap stock isn't always cheap.
What if a company grows its profit fast?
Then a high price to earnings can still be
a bargain.
We measure growth as the yearly rate profits have
climbed.
And we adjust the P E for it, using
the P E G — the P E divided
by the growth rate.

Dixon trades at forty-seven times earnings —
expensive on

the surface. But it grows profits near seventy-seven
percent,
so its P E G is about zero point
six. Below one — cheap for that growth.
Let's put it together on one stock — HDFC
Bank.
Price to earnings, fourteen — cheap for a big
bank.
Price to book, one point eight — fair.
Return on equity, near fourteen percent — solid and
steady.

Low debt, a dividend, and India's most trusted
private
bank.

The verdict from fundamentals alone — a quality
business
at a reasonable price.
But fundamentals never tell you when to buy. For
that, we need the second lens.
Part two. Technicals.
Now we ignore the business, and read only the
price — the trend, the momentum, and the timing.
A price chart is just the story of what
buyers and sellers have agreed on, over time.
Every point is a closing price.
The first thing we read is returns — how
much the price has moved, over a month, six
months, a year.
Up and to the right is an uptrend. Down
is a downtrend. Sideways is indecision.
But raw price is noisy. To see the real
trend, we smooth it.
That smoothing is a moving average.
It's simple — take the last fifty closing prices
and average them. Do that every day, and you
get a smooth line that follows the trend.

Two are famous — the fifty-day and the
two-hundred-day.

The fifty-day is the short-term trend. The
two-hundred-day is
the long-term trend.
The rule of thumb — when the price is

above the two-hundred-day line, the tide is with
you.
Below it, be careful.
Next, momentum — how strong a move is.
The tool is the R S I, a number
from zero to a hundred.
It compares the size of recent gains to recent
losses.
Above seventy, the stock is overbought — it's run
hot and may pause.
Below thirty, it's oversold — beaten down and may
bounce.

Between forty-five and sixty-five is a healthy,
sustainable trend.
The R S I doesn't tell you direction —
it tells you whether a move has gone too
far.
Three risk gauges.

Volatility measures how wildly a price swings, day
to
day. Higher means a bumpier ride.
Beta compares a stock to the whole market —
the Nifty. A beta of one moves with the
market. Above one amplifies it — more reward, more
risk.
And maximum drawdown is the worst fall, from a
peak to a low.
It's the pain you'd have had to sit through.
Knowing it before you buy keeps you honest.
One more, and it's intuitive.

The fifty-two-week range is simply the highest and
lowest
price of the past year.
Where the price sits inside that range tells you
a lot.
Near the high, the stock has momentum — but
less room. Near the low, it's cheap on the
chart — but the trend is weak.
Context, in one glance.
Let's read one chart — Reliance.
The price is below its two-hundred-day line, so the
long-term trend is weak.
Its R S I is around forty-three — neither
overbought nor oversold.
And it sits near the bottom of its yearly
range, at just eight percent.
Its beta is under one, so it's calmer than
the market.
The technical read — a weak tape, but a

beaten-down, low-risk name. The chart says wait; the
fundamentals
said cheap.
Part three. The verdict, and the plan.
We'll turn all these numbers into one call —
then find new stocks, and buy them with discipline.
So how do we decide?
We don't trust any single number.
We score each stock on four independent things —
quality, trend, valuation, and risk — each from zero
to a hundred.
Then we blend them, weighting quality and trend the
most, into one composite score.

Sixty-four or above, accumulate. In the mid-fifties,
add on
dips. In the forties, just hold. Below that, trim.
One number, four honest inputs.

But before any single stock, check the whole
portfolio.
Here's the biggest risk in this real book —
and it isn't any one share.
One holding is almost sixty percent of the money.
So even with seven names, you effectively own only
about two and a half independent bets.

That's concentration. If that one stock stumbles,
the whole
portfolio does.
And it listed less than three weeks ago. Rule
one of investing — don't put all your eggs
in one basket.
Now, finding new stocks.
Two thousand companies trade on the exchange. How do
you get to five?
A funnel.
First, keep only names liquid enough to buy and
sell easily.

Then only sectors that are actually growing —
defence,
electronics, power.
Then only companies with a real record of rising
profits.

Two thousand becomes about forty, then a shortlist
of

twenty-three worth studying — and finally, five
worth buying.
And here they are — five to add, one
a month.

A defence anchor, an electronics leader, a cables
compounder,
and two small-caps with real momentum.
Each scored the same way you just learned.
Higher potential upside — and, to be honest, higher
risk.

These are ideas to research, not promises. Which
brings
us to the hardest question of all.
What is a stock actually worth?
A price target.
Professionals set it three ways.
One — take a fair price to earnings, and
multiply it by next year's expected profit.
Two — average what many analysts expect.
Three — read the chart, where price has found
support and resistance before.

No single method is right. Good analysts triangulate
all
three — and treat the answer as a range,
not a promise.
The honest way to value a stock is to
imagine three futures.
A bad case, where things disappoint. A middle case.
And a good case, where everything goes right.
For each, multiply a fair price to earnings by
expected profit.
Then weight them by how likely each is.
For our top pick, H A L, that weighted
average lands right around today's price.
The bull case is up sixteen percent; the bear
case, down twenty-four.
The lesson — the growth is already in the
price. A double would need the bull case, and
then some.
Finally, how to actually buy — with a plan,
not a panic.
Don't buy everything at once.
Place two orders below the current price, so you
average in as it dips.
These are G T T orders — good, till
triggered. They sit and wait, and only fire when
the price hits your level.
And always place a stop-loss underneath.
If you're wrong, it sells automatically, so one bad
call can only cost so much.
Plan the entry, plan the exit — before emotion
arrives.

Pick one — Hindustan Aeronautics, our
highest-conviction name.

A large-cap defence monopoly that builds India's
fighter jets.

The fundamentals are pristine — zero debt, a
thirty-two

percent return on capital, and the government owns
seventy-two

percent. At thirty-five times earnings, a fair price
for
that quality.

Technically, it sits eleven percent above its
two-hundred-day line
— a healthy uptrend — with a calm beta
near one.
Composite score, eighty-three.
The bull case — Tejas jet deliveries and a
huge order book. The bear case — it all
leans on one buyer.

The plan — average in near forty-six seventy-five,
with
a stop at forty-ninety.

Pick two — Dixon Technologies, India's electronics
factory.

A mid-cap that assembles phones and appliances for
the
world's brands.

The fundamentals are elite — a thirty-seven percent
return

on equity, forty-two on capital. It trades at
forty-eight
times earnings, but with a P-E-G under one, that's
actually cheap for the growth.

The price is nearly twenty percent above its
long-term
average — but a beta of one-and-a-half means a
wild ride, with a forty-seven percent fall in the
past year.
Score, eighty.
Bull — a huge new venture with Vivo. Bear
— thin margins and client concentration.
Buy near fourteen thousand, stop near twelve-one.
Pick three — K-E-I Industries, a cables and wires
compounder.

A mid-cap riding India's electrification and
data-centre boom.

It's debt-free, with a fifteen percent return on
equity

and steady twenty percent returns on capital. At
fifty-three
times earnings, fairly valued for a proven grower.

Technically strong — seventeen percent above its
two-hundred-day line,
near the top of its yearly range.
Score, seventy-one.
Bull — a four-thousand-crore order book and a new

plant by twenty twenty-seven. Bear — export
disruption and
a slower ramp.

Average in near fifty-three-ten, stop at
forty-seven-eighty.
Pick four — Syrma S-G-S, our first small-cap, and
pure momentum.
Another electronics maker, but smaller and faster.

The growth is already printing — revenue up
sixty-eight

percent, profit nearly doubled. But quality is only
moderate

— a fourteen percent return on equity, at
seventy-six
times earnings.
Technically it's the hottest of the five — forty-six

percent above its two-hundred-day line, near its
all-time high,
with a high beta.
Score, seventy-three.

Bull — a sixty-eight-hundred-crore order book. Bear
— a
stretched balance sheet as it grows.

Buy near thirteen seventy-six, stop at
eleven-ninety.

Pick five — Data Patterns, defence electronics, and
the
most expensive of the lot.
A small-cap that builds radar and avionics systems.

It's debt-free, with a twenty-two percent return on
capital

— but at ninety-six times earnings, the valuation
leaves
no room for error; our value score is just
thirty-five.

Technically it's flying — thirty percent above its
long-term
average, up ninety-three percent in a year.
Score, seventy.
Bull — fresh orders, including a radar contract from

B-E-L. Bear — that sky-high multiple and lumpy
timing.

Average in near forty-three-fifty, stop at
thirty-nine-twenty.
Five stocks, one method — now you can read
any of them yourself.
So — how to read a portfolio like a
quant.
Fundamentals tell you if the business is good, and
fairly priced. Technicals tell you what the price is
doing.
Blend four scores into one honest call.
Diversify — concentration is the risk you control.
Treat a target as a range, and always buy
with a stop.
None of this is investment advice — it's a
way of thinking. Learn the tools, then decide for
yourself. Thanks for watching.
